pr_title: Improve text editor status bar and zooming UX
pr_body:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/13228932/0ab33357-1239-4bf1-832e-e11cb9f9c3cd

**Old:**
![Screenshot 2024-02-17 214007](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/13228932/21853a1d-cc2a-4455-b854-48b2672ef042)
**New:**
![Screenshot 2024-02-17 220131](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/13228932/c86dbabe-7073-467a-9962-002f7fcbf5f0)


### Changes
- Text editor zooming no longer triggers a big editor freeze after completion. Fixes #82144.
- Text editor zooming feature now works by adding a multiplier on top of the editor code font size setting, instead of directly modifying the editor setting itself. This is consistent with most modern IDEs.
- The zoom level is now a _transient state_ of each text editor instance. This means for example that it can be different between the script editor and the shader editor, ~and even between each script tab~.
- The zoom level is now displayed in the status bar alongside the line-and-column stats. The zoom level is a clickable `MenuButton` that allows the user to quickly select between a few common zoom levels.
- The status bar now uses of a few `VSeparator`s to separate the various stats, instead of relying on vague empty space and a printed `|` character like before.
- The indentation indicator (`Tabs` / `Spaces`) has been separated from the line-and-column indicators and responds to the appropriate changes (e.g. indentation conversions and editor indentation setting changes), instead of responding to caret changes.
- Some cleanup of code to remove redundancies.

### Rationale
This represents a pretty big change to the role of the zoom feature in the user's workflow. Previously, the zoom feature was a shortcut for making a persistent change to the editor itself, even though it was not obvious to the user that this was happening. It was also easy to accidentally trigger.

In the new system, the zoom feature behaves as a quick, transient operation - similar to a scroll or a drag, while the editor code font size setting serves as the preferred neutral size (at 100% zoom). In this way, the purpose of the zoom feature is to give the user a quick way to navigate their _view_ of a document. ~They are free to leave some documents zoomed out for at-a-glance interaction, while zooming in on others where they are focused on specific areas.~

### Notes
- This is my first time contributing changes that involve the editor interface. Please excuse me if I did some weird things out of ignorance.
- The zoom levels in the popup are chosen arbitrarily based on my own intuition, and are free to change if there is a good reason to.
- ~The zoom levels of each open document are currently _not persistent,_ and will be reset between each session. However, they can totally be saved to the editor cache if we decide that is worthwhile (perhaps in another PR).~
pr_comments: I prefer if all my scripts are at a persistent zoom level and it seems like this will make it hard to do so. Beside this, I fully agree with the approach of not changing a whole editor setting to achieve zooming.

> I prefer if all my scripts are at a persistent zoom level and it seems like this will make it hard to do so. Beside this, I fully agree with the approach of not changing a whole editor setting to achieve zooming.

@MewPurPur Just to clarify, do you mean _persistent_ (saves between sessions), or _consistent_ (synced between all tabs)? Though in truth, making it consistent would actually make it much easier to make it persistent as well, since there is only one value to save to cache. 🤔

I myself am concerned about exposing this `indent_type_changed` signal. It's way too niche, I feel. Consider another way of accomplishing this without requiring the signal. All of these great changes don't look like they should affect the CodeEdit node, but if they have to, they should probably be way more noteworthy than this signal.

> I myself am concerned about exposing this `indent_type_changed` signal. It's way too niche, I feel. Consider another way of accomplishing this without requiring the signal.

@Mickeon I was wondering about that actually. How does one accomplish a subscription-like behaviour in the Godot codebase without the use of signals? Unfortunately there are many places from which the indent type of `CodeEdit` is changed, not all of which are directly within the purview of the script editor.

There are some things in the API that are "exposed" but not really "exposed". These are prefixed with an underscore and do not show up on autocompletion or documentation, and by all means are discouraged to be used. I believe there's _never_ been a case of this for signals, however, so it's probably not supported at all.

So right now, I am not sure how. Again, I'm not against adding more things, but that would warrant people will actually need and use it.

If you want to ask for some help and feedback remember that Godot also has a public chat specifically tailored for development of the engine: https://chat.godotengine.org

Right off the bat, I do have a suggestion. Thinking outside of the box.

A new signal would be much more beneficial if it was emitted on more than one situation, not just when _specifically_ the tab type changes. Resources have a `changed` signal. TileMap also has the `changed` signal as well ~~_(the doc's description is lying to you, what the hell, it is actually emitted in more situations)_~~.
There's many settings that influence **TextEdit**/**CodeEdit**'s behaviour. If they all emitted the same signal on change it would _probably_ be a whole lot more beneficial. 
Performance is not a concern, either, since these settings are unlikely to change very frequently, and the settings' previous values can be cached and checked before acting, anyhow.

However, this suggestion is only somewhat related to this PR, and may require another PR and proposal to be potentially accepted.
It'd be better to first do the less controversial changes in this PR so it's approved more easily.

@Mickeon After doing some more deep studying of the class hierarchy and their interplay, I implemented and pushed a solution which doesn't involve any changes to `CodeEdit`. Would this alleviate your concerns?

It does, **marginally**. Now this feature can be taken a look at without having any interference with the public API, and it can be changed later if necessary.

I for one approve a lot but @MewPurPur made a good point before and it would be nice to see addressed. Never seen a "Per document" zooming level in an IDE (even if it does sound interesting).

My approach would've been to save one value in the editor state, just a script zoom level that'd hold across all scripts. This would be consistent with the current behavior, just no lag spikes from changed editor settings.

Script zoom should definitely be consistent across saves. Persistence is a bonus but not strictly required.

Web browsers store zoom levels on a per-domain basis, but this behavior isn't really suited to code editors.

@Calinou @MewPurPur @Mickeon 

I've added zoom **consistency** between different tabs of each editor. The Script Editor and the Shader Editor each have their own zoom levels, and I think that's a good thing.
![consistent_zoom](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/13228932/e49394fd-11c4-491e-91cd-a3831184c33c)

I've also added **persistence**, implemented through the script and shader editor plugins themselves.
![editor_layout cfg](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/13228932/2810b6cc-759a-4499-bc5e-0c954f225fed)

It was a huge pain to get access to the `CodeTextEditor` (where the zoom functionality is implemented) from the higher-level classes, especially across the two very differently-implemented script and shader systems. But I went for shortest path and added a couple of methods, and did some renamings to avoid ending up with confusing things like
`shader_editor->get_shader_editor()`.

Outstanding job. I hope this gets evaluated soon. The zooming was always a massive pain of the current text editor. It got to the point where @KoBeWi wanted to disable the shortcut outright for accidentally triggering it.

It's not as smooth for me:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/2223172/252253fc-03dc-45ee-859e-79b3df9e9157

Though it's maybe because of dev build. It's still better than before of course and accidental zoom happen in small increments. But I'm still in favor of removing the shortcut >_>

Overall works great, I just found a small bug. When you set 75% zoom and restart, it will be restored as 79%.

> It's not as smooth for me:

That's definitely the dev build. I've also experienced this on dev builds but it wasn't to your extreme. It was also present on dev builds for the old zoom before my changes. But let me know if this isn't the case on your end!

> Overall works great, I just found a small bug. When you set 75% zoom and restart, it will be restored as 79%.

This is actually intended behaviour. The zoom factor is always corrected to the nearest font size. It will not always land on a nice round number like the presets. This makes sure the zooming happens in consistent steps of 1 font size each. When you first select a zoom preset from the dropdown, it forces a label change to match the exact text you clicked, otherwise it looks like too much of a bug. But when you zoom with the shortcuts again, or restart, it will revert to displaying the actual ground truth zoom factor. This is also how Visual Studio behaves.

The alternative is that zooming happens in bigger increments and we don't correct the zoom factor to the nearest font size. This would result in bigger, more uneven zooming, with some font sizes being skipped, and potentially bigger accidental skips.

> This is actually intended behaviour. The zoom factor is always corrected to the nearest font size.

This makes sense but it definitely does not look correct. I can imagine an unknowing user being ever so slightly bothered by this to open an issue. Not sure what the exact solution could be.
Maybe the display is rounded down to the specific percentage (e.g. `79%` -> `75%`)?
Alternatively the way the zoom is displayed could be re-evaluated? Visual Studio Code displays an lens icon if the whole editor is zoomed in or out. But that's not something done anywhere in Godot, where the percentage is much more common.

> > This is actually intended behaviour. The zoom factor is always corrected to the nearest font size.
> 
> This makes sense but it definitely does not look correct. I can imagine an unknowing user being ever so slightly bothered by this to open an issue. Not sure what the exact solution could be. Maybe the display is rounded down to the specific percentage (e.g. `79%` -> `75%`)? Alternatively the way the zoom is displayed could be re-evaluated? Visual Studio Code displays an lens icon if the whole editor is zoomed in or out. But that's not something done anywhere in Godot, where the percentage is much more common.

@Mickeon 
Rounding isn't an option because there is no rounding interval which is simultaneously:
- big enough to mask cases like this one.
- small enough to always show a change when you zoom (lack of UI feedback)

I'm a little unclear as to what your second alternative was, could you explain that one again?

One solution I can propose is to bypass the scale factor correction itself when setting to one of the presets, instead of just masking with a display change. I will try that.

@Mickeon @KoBeWi 
I've changed `CodeTextEditor::set_zoom_factor`, and now the presets will now display properly when closing and restarting the editor. Thanks for catching that.
@KoBeWi Did the rebase! Should be ready to go. 🤞
Thanks!

issue_context.title: lagging when zooming a script using Distraction Free Mode
issue_context.body:
### Godot version

4.1.1.stable

### System information

Godot v4.1.1.stable - Windows 10.0.19045 - Vulkan (Mobile) - dedicated NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 (NVIDIA; 31.0.15.3734) - Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-9400F CPU @ 2.90GHz (6 Threads)

### Issue description


The program is lagging when I zoom out in a script using Distraction Free Mode. The script was just a CharacterBody2D script using the Basic Movement template. 
The program even crashed once, though I'm having trouble reproducing the crash, but I can reproduce the script editor lag.

My project is very initial, I created it yesterday. 
![godot-script](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/94930303/eff3bf52-e4ee-4726-907c-a0b0c316c92c)


### Steps to reproduce

Toggle "Distraction Free Mode" in the script editor.
Zoom in (or out) some times (you'll notice the program becomes laggy).
Optionally, if you click anywhere on the script to start typing, you'll notice it will lag for a few seconds.


### Minimal reproduction project

[ScriptLagTest.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/12704157/ScriptLagTest.zip)
comments:
I can confirm this on 4.2.dev 7831eedf1 (Linux, GeForce RTX 4090):

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/180032/74f3da82-fbba-4442-acbd-7faedaedf36b

This occurs regardless of whether distraction-free mode is enabled. It can also be reproduced at relatively low font sizes (by hiDPI standards) such as 25.

This is likely because all editor settings are occasionally reloaded when there's no need to (which is also what happens when you change editor theme settings or colors, for instance).

If I were to guess, it's because zooming in/out actually changes the font size in the editor settings. So `EDITOR_THEME_CHANGED` and likely `EDITOR_SETTINGS_CHANGED` fire, causing a lot of code to propagate and resulting in extreme slowdowns.

Maybe we have some opportunities to somehow speed up editor theme changes? Or to localize impacts? @YuriSizov has probably thought about this stuff before

Hi there, just wanted to add my two cents, since I came to add a similar proposal and saw this one.

I actually use zoom in/out all the time as part of my coding process in Visual Studio. It's important to me to be able to see my code at whatever level of detail I need. Sometimes I like to see more of the "big picture", and sometimes I like to really focus in on a small section.

I think what struck me as odd is that script editor zoom (and shader editor zoom) was implemented as an font size preference, instead of as a zoom scale applied on top and saved in the `.godot` folder or something. For comparison, you can zoom in the 3D viewport, and that is also saved, but it is saved differently and doesn't require a slow save/refresh.

Could text zoom potentially be implemented that way instead?

> Could text zoom potentially be implemented that way instead?

Fonts are rasterized, they aren't rendered in vector in realtime. This is different from the 3D environment, which is rendered based on the spatial information. So, no, without a significant rework of how fonts work in general this isn't possible.

> > Could text zoom potentially be implemented that way instead?
> 
> Fonts are rasterized, they aren't rendered in vector in realtime. This is different from the 3D environment, which is rendered based on the spatial information. So, no, without a significant rework of how fonts work in general this isn't possible.

What I meant is not to change the render method, but rather change what the "role" of a zoom change is.

You can still make it increment as a font size "offset" without treating it as an editor preference change. And consequently, without needing to trigger a whole preference save or theme refresh.

I did a quick tool script implementation to show what I mean. The "font size offset" is just implemented as a font size override that can optionally be saved to the project cache or editor cache or whatever. It's an ephemeral state on top of the long-term editor setting. You can just reset it to zero, and it will show the underlying font size as per the editor settings.

![font_size_override](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/13228932/08243611-819d-4d99-8a5d-a70aed122961)

EDIT: Here's an alternate take on that which uses a zoom percentage instead of an integer offset, for something more understandable to the user (this is how Visual Studio works):
![font_scale](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/13228932/821d5d2b-996c-4634-8962-263171a86927)
Hi all, I made a PR #88474 which (among other things) has a fix for this. Please take a look and give your thoughts. Thanks! :)

review_comments: If you need to set text to match selected option, sounds like OptionButton would be better. You can make it flat to look the same.
OptionButton, even flat, has an arrow on it and I cannot find a good way to hide.
Assign empty ImageTexture as override for `arrow`.

I remembered the other reason I chose a MenuButton is because the text isn't always a reflection of the selected text, and in fact, there isn't even always a selection. So constantly managing the text override and the selection index when there's a custom zoom (which is most of the time), was less straightforward than just using a MenuButton, which is what a lot of things in the editor's bars use.

Unless there's another good reason not to use a MenuButton I'm gonna mark this one as resolved.

What's the rename for? (other than unifying the code I guess)
Since the change is rather significant, it's something that should be done in a separate PR, unless it's important for something.

This is the case which I said was to reduce confusion. The variable isn't exposed so I thought it would be fine to rename.

The containing class is `TextShaderEditor`, and is referred to by the plugin as `shader_editor`. This is fine, it's an editor of text shaders, so it's ultimately a shader editor. However the class also itself contains a variable called `shader_editor`. It also happens to be the variable I needed to expose. It would've resulted in `shader_editor.get_shader_editor()`. This variable's type is `ShaderTextEditor`, which is a subclass of `CodeTextEditor`. It's ultimately an editor of code. So a good renaming is to make it consistent with other classes on the script side of things, and call it a `code_editor`.

With this in mind, should I still move the variable rename to a different PR? I would like to at least keep the naming of the function I added `(get_code_editor)`.

@KoBeWi I've fixed your other reviews. For this one, could you explain to me the rationale behind shying away from renaming a private variable like this? And if we absolutely have to keep the old name for the private var, is it okay if we have a `get_code_editor()` method that returns a var called `shader_editor`?
This change creates noise in the diff, but since there weren't other significant changes in that file, maybe it's fine in the end.
